title: Echinacea
subtitle: The short-course immune herb taken at the first sign of a cold
excerpt: Echinacea is the most-used immune herb in western herbal practice, traditionally taken at the first sign of a cold or infection as a short course of seven to fourteen days. It modulates immune activity rather than simply stimulating it, and carries important cautions for anyone with an autoimmune condition.
sourceNotes: Felter and Lloyd, King's American Dispensatory (1898), echinacea entry, public domain. Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), echinacea entry, Botanical.com transcription. EMA HMPC monograph on Echinacea purpurea herb (2015), open access, safety and course-length reference. WHO Monographs on Selected Medicinal Plants, Volume 1 (1999), Herba Echinaceae Purpureae monograph, open access. Cochrane Review: Karsch-Volk M et al., Echinacea for preventing and treating the common cold, 2015.

glossaryTerms.definition: An action that adjusts and regulates the activity of the immune system. Not the same as simply stimulating it: modulation can mean raising or lowering immune activity depending on what the body needs.
A group of compounds in echinacea root and aerial parts associated with the tingling sensation on the tongue and with the herb's immune-modulating action.
The daisy family. Includes echinacea, chamomile, calendula, yarrow, and ragweed. Readers with a known allergy to ragweed, daisies, or chrysanthemums should patch-test or avoid all Asteraceae herbs.

content.text: Echinacea in the home kitchen is the alcohol extract or tea kept for the first sign of a cold: a short course of seven to fourteen days rather than a daily supplement. The distinction matters. Echinacea is
immune-modulating

, not simply immune-stimulating, and the traditional application is an acute short course at the onset of infection, not continuous long-term use. The root alcohol extract keeps two years in a dark cupboard; dried herb for tea keeps a year.
Precautions
Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms.

Autoimmune conditions: echinacea modulates immune activity. Readers with lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, or any other autoimmune condition should consult a herbalist before using echinacea, because altering immune activity in an already dysregulated immune system is not straightforward.

Not for long-term continuous use: the traditional and regulatory guidance is to use echinacea as short acute courses of seven to fourteen days, not continuously. Continuous use is not the standard in any tradition and is not supported by the available evidence.
Allergen note: echinacea is a member of the
Asteraceae family

(the daisy family). Readers with a documented allergy to ragweed, chamomile, calendula, or chrysanthemums should approach echinacea with caution. Allergic reactions to echinacea, including anaphylaxis in sensitised individuals, are documented. If you have any Asteraceae allergy, consult a doctor before using this herb.
Botanical

Echinacea purpurea, family Asteraceae. The purple coneflower is a tall, robust perennial with distinctive cone-shaped central discs and drooping purple-pink ray petals. Parts used are the aerial parts (leaf, stem, flower) and the root. the aerial parts give different constituent profiles from the root. Commercial preparations use both. Two other species are also in common use: Echinacea angustifolia (narrow-leaved coneflower). Which is native to the North American prairies and was the species used most extensively in Eclectic American herbal medicine, and Echinacea pallida. Echinacea purpurea is the easiest to grow in the UK garden and the most widely studied in modern trials.
active compounds and actions

The main active compounds fall into three groups. Alkylamides in the root cause the distinctive tingling on the tongue and are the best-extracted in alcohol. Polysaccharides in the aerial parts are linked to activity on immune cells when extracted in water. Caffeic acid derivatives (including echinacoside) are higher in E. angustifolia and E. pallida roots. The overall picture is one of immune modulation. More a shift in immune activity than a simple stimulation.
Traditional uses

Native American traditions were the first to use the plant as medicine. The Eclectic American tradition of the 1800s took it up extensively. Using it for infections, septic conditions, and as an all-purpose immune herb. The King's American Dispensatory gives extensive coverage of echinacea, noting its wide use for infections of all kinds. Wound infections, and blood-poisoning presentations.

Western herbal practice adopted echinacea in the twentieth century, where it became established as the standard short-course herb at the onset of a cold or flu. The specific framing in modern western herbal practice is an acute course of seven to fourteen days. Started at the first sign of infection: sore throat, sneezing, the sense that something is coming on. It is not used as a permanent preventive supplement in the tradition.
Preparations

A alcohol extract of echinacea root or aerial parts in 40% spirit is the most common modern preparation: 2 to 4 ml in a small glass of water, two to three times a day for up to fourteen days. The tingling sensation on the tongue from the alkylamides is often considered a quality marker for root alcohol extract: if the alcohol extract doesn't tingle. The alkylamide content may be low

A tea of dried herb is the older preparation: one teaspoon per cup, steeped for ten minutes, up to three times a day. The tea extracts the polysaccharides well. The alkylamides from the root extract better in alcohol than in water.
Cautions and cautions
Autoimmune conditions: speak to a herbalist first. Echinacea may not suit you if your immune system is already affected by a long-term health condition such as lupus or multiple sclerosis.

Course length: echinacea is not for continuous daily use. Use it as a short course of seven to fourteen days at the onset of infection and then stop. If you want to use it again, take a break of at least the same length before starting another course.
Asteraceae allergy: echinacea is in the daisy family. Any known allergy to ragweed, chamomile, or daisies is a reason to consult a doctor first.
Pregnancy: echinacea has not been studied enough in pregnancy. Consult a herbalist or your midwife before using it during pregnancy.
